```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 3.2, fig.align = "center")
library(karma2d)
```

This vignette explains how `karma2d_simulate()` generates images, how its
random-number handling works, how to run a (toy) Monte Carlo study, and how
the choice and reliability of the information matrix affect inference.

## The simulation scheme

`karma2d_simulate()` draws images from the conditional model on an **extended
grid** of size $(N + b)\times(M + b)$, where $b$ is the `burn_in`, and
returns the last $N$ rows and $M$ columns. With $w = \max(p, q)$:

1. The first $w$ rows and columns of the extended grid are initialised with
   $g(y) = \alpha$ and $e = 0$.
2. The remaining pixels are generated row by row. For each pixel the linear
   predictor $\eta[n,m]$ is computed from the already generated neighbours,
   $\mu[n,m] = g^{-1}(\eta[n,m])$, and the pixel is drawn by the inverse
   transform $y = Q(u;\mu,\varphi)$ with $u\sim U(0,1)$ (`qkuma()`).
3. The error $e[n,m] = g(y[n,m]) - \eta[n,m]$ is stored for the MA terms.

The default `burn_in` is $2w$, which reproduces the scheme of the original
scripts of the article. A longer burn-in reduces the influence of the
artificial initial values. No claim is made that the simulated process is
stationary for arbitrary coefficients: if a pixel becomes numerically 0 or 1
the function stops with an informative error.

```{r simulate}
y <- karma2d_simulate(30, 30, alpha = 0.3, ar = c(0.3, 0.2, -0.1),
                      shape = 8, seed = 11)
dim(y)
str(attr(y, "karma2d"))
```

```{r image}
image(t(y[rev(seq_len(nrow(y))), ]), col = hcl.colors(32, "viridis"),
      axes = FALSE,
      main = "KARMA(1,0), 30 x 30")
```

Images on another support are obtained with `lower` and `upper`; the model is
fitted with the same arguments:

```{r support}
y2 <- karma2d_simulate(20, 20, alpha = 0.1, ar = c(0.2, 0.1, 0), shape = 6,
                       lower = -1, upper = 1, seed = 5)
range(y2)
```

### The `seed` argument leaves the global RNG alone

When `seed` is given, the function sets the seed internally and restores the
caller's random-number state afterwards, so simulating does not change what
the rest of your script draws.

```{r seed}
set.seed(123)
before <- .Random.seed
a <- karma2d_simulate(15, 15, alpha = 0.2, ar = c(0.2, 0.1, 0.1),
                      shape = 5, seed = 1)
identical(.Random.seed, before)   # the global stream is untouched
b <- karma2d_simulate(15, 15, alpha = 0.2, ar = c(0.2, 0.1, 0.1),
                      shape = 5, seed = 1)
identical(a, b)                    # and the result is reproducible
```

If `seed = NULL` the function uses (and advances) the global generator, so
`set.seed()` before the call works as usual.

## A toy Monte Carlo study

The code below runs 20 replications of a 20 x 20 KARMA(1, 0) model and
summarizes mean, bias, mean squared error (MSE) and the empirical coverage of
95% Wald intervals. **This is only an illustration of the workflow**: 20
replications are far too few to judge bias or coverage. Full simulation
studies are described in `vignette("reproducing-the-paper")`.

```{r monte-carlo}
truth <- c(alpha = 0.3, `phi(0,1)` = 0.3, `phi(1,0)` = 0.2,
           `phi(1,1)` = -0.1, shape = 8)
n_rep <- 20
est <- matrix(NA_real_, n_rep, length(truth),
              dimnames = list(NULL, names(truth)))
cover <- est
for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {
  y <- karma2d_simulate(20, 20, alpha = truth[["alpha"]], ar = truth[2:4],
                        shape = truth[["shape"]], seed = 1000 + r)
  fit <- karma2d_fit(y, order = c(1, 0))
  ci <- confint(fit, level = 0.95)
  est[r, ] <- coef(fit)
  cover[r, ] <- ci[, 1] <= truth & truth <= ci[, 2]
}
summary_table <- data.frame(
  truth = truth,
  mean = colMeans(est),
  bias = colMeans(est) - truth,
  MSE = colMeans(sweep(est, 2, truth)^2),
  coverage = colMeans(cover)
)
round(summary_table, 4)
```

With 20 replications the coverage can only take values that are multiples of
0.05, and its Monte Carlo standard error is around 5 percentage points.

### Parallel streams

For larger studies, use independent random-number streams per worker. The
`seed` argument of `karma2d_simulate()` takes a single number, so the usual
approach is one seed per replication; alternatively, use L'Ecuyer-CMRG
streams from the `parallel` package and simulate with `seed = NULL`. This
chunk is not evaluated here.

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
library(parallel)
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(2024)
seeds <- vector("list", 100)
seeds[[1]] <- .Random.seed
for (i in 2:100) seeds[[i]] <- nextRNGStream(seeds[[i - 1]])

one_rep <- function(i) {
  assign(".Random.seed", seeds[[i]], envir = globalenv())
  y <- karma2d_simulate(25, 25, alpha = 0.3, ar = c(0.3, 0.2, -0.1),
                        shape = 8)          # seed = NULL: uses the stream
  coef(karma2d_fit(y, order = c(1, 0)))
}
res <- mclapply(seq_along(seeds), one_rep, mc.cores = 4)
```

## Expected versus observed information

Standard errors come from the inverse of an information matrix evaluated at
the estimates. `karma2d_control(information = )` selects which one:

* `"expected"` (default): the conditional Fisher information, in closed form
  (see `vignette("model-theory")`).
* `"observed"`: minus the Hessian of the log-likelihood, obtained by central
  differences of the analytic score.

```{r information}
y <- karma2d_simulate(30, 30, alpha = 0.3, ar = c(0.3, 0.2, -0.1),
                      shape = 8, seed = 11)
fit_e <- karma2d_fit(y, c(1, 0))
fit_o <- karma2d_fit(y, c(1, 0),
                     control = karma2d_control(information = "observed"))
all.equal(coef(fit_e), coef(fit_o))   # same point estimates
rbind(expected = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_e))),
      observed = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_o))))
```

The point estimates are identical; only the standard errors, Wald tests and
confidence intervals differ. Both are asymptotic approximations; on small
images they may differ noticeably, in particular for the shape parameter. The
information of any fit can be recomputed afterwards with
`karma2d_fisher(fit, type = "observed")`.

## When the information matrix is not usable

The covariance matrix is only computed when the information matrix is
numerically positive definite. The package **never regularises** it
silently: if the matrix is not positive definite, `vcov()` is filled with
`NA`, a warning is emitted and the reason is stored in `fit$inference`.
If it is positive definite but nearly singular, the covariance is computed but
flagged `"ill-conditioned"` with a warning.

The following very small, almost constant image (so that the parameters are
barely identifiable) illustrates the second situation:

```{r ill-conditioned}
set.seed(1)
y_flat <- matrix(runif(64, 0.45, 0.55), 8, 8)
fit_bad <- withCallingHandlers(
  karma2d_fit(y_flat, order = c(1, 1)),
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Warning captured: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
fit_bad$inference$status
```

The helper that implements the rule can be applied directly to any matrix; for
a matrix that is not positive definite the covariance is `NA`:

```{r non-pd}
not_pd <- matrix(c(1, 2, 2, 1), 2)     # eigenvalues 3 and -1
res <- withCallingHandlers(
  karma2d:::covariance_from_information(not_pd),
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Warning captured: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
res$status
res$vcov
```

`summary()` repeats the warning and states that Wald inference should not be
trusted. In practice, a non-positive-definite information matrix usually
points to an over-parametrised model for the image size, a poorly converged
fit (check `fit$convergence` and the BFGS message in
`karma2d_diagnostics(fit)`), or an image with almost no variability.
